description: We’re building a research tool that helps people find and compare NASA’s microgravity fire experiments and trace AI explanations back to the original evidence.
summary:
Fire behaves differently in space, and the next crewed habitats will breathe air that almost no fire test has covered. A Moon base or rover is planned around 30% oxygen at 10.2 psi; NASA's combustion archive holds only 8 table rows tested near that atmosphere, all in microgravity. The evidence that exists is scattered across 24 investigations, about 2,000 table rows and separate report PDFs, and the sources sometimes disagree.

Flaregrain is a web app that lets anyone ask a plain-language question about NASA's microgravity fire experiments and get an answer they can check. It finds the closest NASA records and report pages, a small open model writes a short summary from them, and a checker keeps only the sentences that match the NASA facts they cite. Every sentence links to its NASA page. Compare puts two experiments side by side, and Fire beyond Earth shows what NASA tested near each habitat atmosphere and what nobody has tested yet.

It matters because fire-safety decisions for Moon and Mars habitats will lean on this evidence, and a tool that summarises it must never blur what NASA measured with what a model wrote.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flaregrain answers questions about NASA's microgravity fire experiments for people planning fire safety in spacecraft and in Moon and Mars habitats.

Ask: type a question. The page shows its work in stages (searching, sources found, writing, checking), then a short summary. Each sentence links to the NASA page behind it, and quoted excerpts from those pages sit underneath.

Compare: two experiments side by side, with what they share, how they differ and what the sources leave open.

Fire beyond Earth: seven habitat atmospheres, from ISS cabin air to a Moon base. For each, it shows how many NASA tests ran nearby and what is untested. For a Moon base or rover (30% oxygen, 10.2 psi) that is 8 table rows, all from one investigation, all in microgravity.

WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT

Every NASA value links to its report page or table. Where two NASA sources disagree, both values are shown.

The model may only use numbered facts from the sources it was given. A rule-based checker removes any sentence with a wrong number, a wrong record or no citation, and the page says how many it removed.

Model text is always labelled as an AI summary, never as NASA evidence.

IT CAUGHT OUR OWN MISTAKE

Our hand-written answer to "How long did the flame take to go out after airflow was cut?" said the sources give no elapsed time. When we sent that question through the model instead, it cited a page of NASA's BASS-II report that we had missed: the flame went out within 2 seconds of an abrupt cutoff. The checker passed the sentence, we read the page, and we corrected the site the same afternoon.

HOW WE BUILT IT, AND WITH WHAT AI

The team of four directed the work and checked the NASA values by hand. AI coding assistants (Claude Code and Codex) wrote most of the code under our review. The model that writes answers is qwen3:4b, an open model running on a team member's own computer, not a paid AI service. No AI-generated images or video are used; the site's visuals are drawn by code, and the demo video is a screen recording.

UNDER THE HOOD

Data: NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics combustion archive (24 investigations, 2,009 table rows) and 9 NASA reports. The intake checksums each file and normalizes 24,573 values, 575 of them flagged. 13 records were checked by hand against the original report pages.

Retrieval: keyword ranking over the checked records and 1,321 report passages, always the same for the same question. The full dashboard's ranking of investigations measures recall@5 0.850 and hit@1 0.833 over 108 scored question wordings.

Checker: 139 saved explanations, 492 sentences kept and 270 removed. A stress test of 343,758 synthetic sentences found 0 misses for wrong numbers or wrong records; it has a known gap for invented details.

Tools: Python 3, Node.js, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js, Ollama with qwen3:4b, Playwright, Vercel, GitHub, Tailscale.

LIMITS

The public site carries 13 hand-checked records; the full dataset is summarised on Fire beyond Earth and System design. Mars values are assumptions and are labelled so.
